reason: A cereal after a cereal shares stemborers, Striga (witchweed) and leaf diseases, and both draw heavily on soil nitrogen.
A legume after a cereal breaks the cereal pest and disease cycle and can leave some nitrogen for the next crop.
Cereals can use nitrogen left by a legume and are not hurt by legume root diseases.
Legumes share root rots, nematodes and pod pests. Repeating them builds these problems up.
Tomatoes after tomatoes, potatoes or related crops build up bacterial wilt, blight and nematodes.
Kale after kale or cabbage builds up clubroot, black rot and diamondback moth.
Root and tuber crops back to back build up weevils, viruses and nematodes, and both draw heavily on potassium.
Vegetables with a high nitrogen demand benefit from nitrogen left by a legume.
Root crops need little added nitrogen, so they follow legumes without difficulty.
Different family and rooting depth from the cereal, which breaks cereal pest cycles.
Different family from the root crop. Cereals can use soil loosened by harvesting roots, but need nitrogen.
A legume after a root crop breaks pest cycles and can help restore nitrogen.
Different family from the vegetable crop. Cereals suit the residual fertility left by well-fed vegetables.
A legume after vegetables breaks pest cycles and uses residual fertility.
Different family from the cereal, but vegetables are demanding and the cereal may have used up nitrogen.
Vegetables from different families can follow each other, but demands on the soil stay high.
